desc: The Western Ghats Escarpment is a 1,500 km long mountain range along the western coast of India, running from Gujarat to Kerala. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the eight hottest biodiversity hotspots in the world. The escarpment rises abruptly from the narrow coastal plain, reaching heights of over 2,600 meters. It forms a major watershed, intercepting the southwest monsoon rains and creating rain shadow conditions in the Deccan plateau to the east. The escarpment is older than the Himalayas and contains some of India's most pristine evergreen forests and highest rainfall zones.
fact: It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the eight hottest biodiversity hotspots · It runs 1,500 km along India's western coast from Gujarat to Kerala · It intercepts the southwest monsoon, creating a rain shadow in the Deccan plateau · It is older than the Himalayas with peaks over 2,600 meters

desc: The Eastern Ghats Escarpment is a discontinuous mountain range along the eastern coast of India, spanning Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka. Unlike the continuous Western Ghats, the Eastern Ghats are broken into separate blocks by major rivers flowing eastward. The escarpment reaches heights of about 1,600 meters at its highest peak, Arma Konda in Andhra Pradesh. The range is composed of ancient metamorphic rocks and is rich in mineral resources including bauxite and manganese. The Eastern Ghats support tropical deciduous forests and are home to tribal communities including the Khond and Savara.
fact: The Eastern Ghats are a discontinuous escarpment along India's eastern coast · The range is broken by major east-flowing rivers · The highest peak is Arma Konda at 1,600 meters · The escarpment is rich in bauxite and manganese mineral deposits

desc: The Saharanpur Escarpment, also known as the Siwalik Hills escarpment, marks the southern boundary of the Siwalik range at the transition from the Himalayan foothills to the Indo-Gangetic plains. It rises abruptly by about 300-500 meters above the plains. The escarpment is composed of young sedimentary rocks deposited by ancient Himalayan rivers. It is a seismically active zone and marks the Main Frontal Thrust of the Himalaya. The foothill forests along the escarpment are important wildlife corridors connecting the lowlands with higher Himalayan reserves.
fact: It marks the southern boundary of the Siwalik Hills rising 300-500 meters above the plains · It is composed of young sedimentary Himalayan river deposits · It marks the Main Frontal Thrust, a seismically active tectonic zone · The foothill forests serve as important wildlife corridors

desc: The Great Escarpment of Central India includes the Satpura and Vindhya ranges that separate northern India from the Deccan plateau. These escarpments rise to heights of about 600-1,350 meters and stretch across central India for over 1,000 km. The Satpura Range forms the northern boundary of the Deccan plateau with steep escarpments facing both north and south. The ranges are composed of ancient Deccan Trap basalt and Gondwana sedimentary rocks. They contain important wildlife sanctuaries and national parks including Satpura and Kanha. The escarpments are the source of major rivers including the Narmada and Tapti.
fact: The Satpura and Vindhya escarpments separate northern India from the Deccan plateau · They stretch over 1,000 km across central India · They contain Satpura and Kanha national parks · The Narmada and Tapti rivers originate from these escarpments

desc: The Siwalik Hills Escarpment runs along the entire Himalayan foothill belt from Jammu to Arunachal Pradesh. It forms the outermost range of the Himalayas, rising abruptly from the Indo-Gangetic plains. The escarpment is composed of conglomerates, sandstones, and mudstones deposited in the foreland basin of the rising Himalayas over the last 5 million years. It is the youngest mountain range in the Himalaya system. The escarpment is famous for its abundant fossil deposits of prehistoric mammals including ancestral elephants, horses, and apes. The Siwalik forests are biodiversity-rich corridors for wildlife including tigers and elephants.
fact: It is the youngest mountain range in the Himalaya system, formed over 5 million years · It runs along the entire Himalayan foothill belt from Jammu to Arunachal Pradesh · It is famous for abundant fossil deposits including ancestral elephants and apes · The forests along the escarpment serve as wildlife corridors for tigers and elephants
